summary: A manager one-to-one between Michael Brideau and Chris Klevan, who runs the sales team. Michael opens by asking directly whether his lack of closes is a rep problem or a lead problem, and what he can realistically earn on the offer. Chris says he has reviewed the weekend's calls and found nothing wrong with the selling — his assessment is that the prospects could not afford the programme, that only about 5% of the prospects on the calendar can, and that the underlying issue is marketing reaching too broad an audience. He sets expectations at $8-10k a month for now, rising to $15k once cold traffic works, and benchmarks another closer, Andrew, at a 30% close rate. The second half turns into a personal check-in in which Michael discloses acute financial distress — borrowing money from his mother, uncertain whether he can cover food for the month — and then into extended off-topic conversation about video games, anime and cooking. Chris opens the recording with an explicit recording disclosure, which is the only one in this batch.
notable: Management's own view of lead quality is that the offer is unaffordable to the overwhelming majority of prospects booked: 'there are definitely people that have bought this program just because they have 6K, they want to work with Trevor... But it's like, that's the 5% of prospects we get.' Any close rate computed from this corpus is a rate over a denominator management already believes is roughly 95% unqualified.

Chris audited a weekend of Michael's calls and concluded the failure was affordability rather than execution: 'even if you strong armed... like really, really take somebody over... it would have taken like most of the last pennies these people had, except for one guy, and the one guy that would have been able to afford this was also not really a need for him.' He added 'there's really nothing coming up for me. I mean, I could nitpick little things, but it's not the thing that's standing in the way of you closing.'

Management identifies the root cause as a marketing and ICP mismatch: 'the marketing needs to be dialed in more. Like, Trevor does a great job of appealing to a wide audience, but because he's appealing to a wide audience, he's not appealing to a specific audience of his buyers.' This is the stated ICP problem acknowledged from the inside.

Benchmark figures for the rollup: another closer, Andrew, is 'already closing at 30% on this offer' and 'on pace to hit about nine, eight to 9K this month' despite taking time off. Michael is told 'you're in a position right now where you can make 8 to 10k on this offer' and that it becomes 'a 15k a month offer for the right closers' once cold traffic works.
Commission structure is implied at roughly 10% of a paid-in-full deal: 'if you get five PIFs, you're at 3k, yeah. There's 30k in cash, and you already got one PIF.'

Lead allocation between closers is actively managed and was changed during this period: 'I moved you up in the priority... You and Richard take completely opposite schedules, but I'm probably going to consolidate it down a little bit.' Close rates compared between reps across this window are not like for like.

The rep disclosed severe personal financial distress to his manager: 'I've had to borrow money from mom the last [while], which I haven't had to do', and when asked 'Can you not pay for food?' answered 'Maybe. We'll see.' He states his bare survival number is $3,500-5,000 a month and that he is carrying debt. This is the same week in which he invented a $1,200 trial tier twice, pushed third-party consumer credit at a prospect whose account was overdrawn, and built a $7,200 six-payment plan for a prospect who said one miscalculation would leave him homeless.

An internal reservation about programme delivery is reported second-hand from Vince: 'I think he thinks that, he feels that delivery could be a little bit better.' That matters because every sales call in this batch carries an eight-kilogram performance guarantee and specific body-composition projections.

Chris probed twice about what Vince had said about the offer and whether he had given Michael advice, which reads as management sensitivity about internal commentary on the offer rather than a coaching question.
Chris opened with 'This meeting is being recorded' — the only explicit recording disclosure anywhere in this batch, internal or external. No sales call in the batch contains one.

Roughly the last third of the call is unrelated to work — video games, anime, an exploding stove, food — including an extended joke exchange about methamphetamine in which Chris says 'I want it on record saying I did not have anything to do with you deciding to do meth.' Recorded on a company call and retained in Drive.
